claim: Structural and functional studies of the ATP-binding cassette transporter MsbA have revealed two distinct lipopolysaccharide (LPS) binding sites: one located in the central cavity and the other at a membrane-facing, exterior site.
source: Structural and functional studies of the ATP-binding cassette transporter MsbA have revealed two distinct lipopolysaccharide (LPS) binding sites: one located in the central cavity and the other at a membrane-facing, exterior site.
evidence: This is a statement about prior structural and functional studies that identified two LPS binding sites on MsbA, supported by references to existing literature.

claim: The binding of KDL is solely driven by entropy, despite the transporter adopting an inward-facing conformation or trapped in an outward-facing conformation with adenosine 5'-diphosphate and vanadate.
source: The binding of KDL is solely driven by entropy, despite the transporter adopting an inward-facing conformation or trapped in an outward-facing conformation with adenosine 5'-diphosphate and vanadate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from native mass spectrometry measurements at different temperatures showing thermodynamic parameters.

claim: The molecular recognition of KDL is driven by a positive coupling entropy (as large as –100 kJ/mol at 298 K) that outweighs unfavorable coupling enthalpy.
source: We find the molecular recognition of KDL is driven by a positive coupling entropy (as large as –100 kJ/mol at 298 K) that outweighs unfavorable coupling enthalpy.
evidence: This is supported by mutant cycle analysis data presented in the manuscript showing coupling thermodynamic parameters.

claim: Alterations in solvent reorganization and conformational entropy can contribute significantly to the free energy of protein-lipid association.
source: These findings indicate that alterations in solvent reorganization and conformational entropy can contribute significantly to the free energy of protein-lipid association.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the thermodynamic data showing large entropic contributions to binding.

claim: Most Gram-negative bacteria contain outer membrane lipopolysaccharide (LPS) that is crucial for maintaining structural integrity and protection from toxins and antibiotics.
source: Most Gram-negative bacteria contain outer membrane lipopolysaccharide (LPS) that is crucial for maintaining structural integrity and protection from toxins and antibiotics (Simpson and Trent, 2019; Raetz and Whitfield, 2002; Raetz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Gram-negative bacteria supported by citations.

claim: The ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter MsbA flips an LPS-precursor, lipooligosaccharide (LOS), from the cytosolic leaflet to the periplasmic leaflet of inner membrane, a process powered by the hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
source: The ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter MsbA flips an LPS-precursor, lipooligosaccharide (LOS), from the cytosolic leaflet to the periplasmic leaflet of inner membrane, a process powered by the hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
evidence: This describes the known function of MsbA based on established literature.

claim: MsbA functions as a homodimer and each subunit consists of a soluble nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) and a transmembrane domain containing six transmembrane helices.
source: MsbA functions as a homodimer and each subunit consists of a soluble nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) and a transmembrane domain containing six transmembrane helices (Rees et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established structural information about MsbA supported by citation.

claim: The ATPase activity of MsbA can be stimulated in the presence of different substrates, particularly hexaacylated lipid A species.
source: Like other ABC transporters, the ATPase activity of MsbA can be stimulated in the presence of different substrates, particularly hexaacylated lipid A species. (Doerrler and Raetz, 2002; Eckford and Sharom, 2008; Siarheyeva and Sharom, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing substrate-stimulated ATPase activity.

claim: The interior binding site is located in the inner cavity, and mutations (R78A, R148A and K299A) engineered to disrupt binding at this site abolish lipid-stimulated ATPase activity and adversely affect cell growth.
source: The interior binding site is located in the inner cavity, and mutations (R78A, R148A and K299A) engineered to disrupt binding at this site abolish lipid-stimulated ATPase activity and adversely affect cell growth. (Mi et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that characterized the interior binding site and effects of mutations.

claim: The LPS-precursor 3-deoxy-D-manno-oct-2-ulosonic (Kdo)2-lipid A (KDL) was found to bind to an elusive exterior site on MsbA trapped in an OF conformation with adenosine 5'-diphosphate and vanadate.
source: More recently, the LPS-precursor 3-deoxy-D-manno-oct-2-ulosonic (Kdo)2-lipid A (KDL) was found to bind to an elusive exterior site on MsbA trapped in an OF conformation with adenosine 5'-diphosphate and vanadate (Doerrler and Raetz, 2002; Eckford and Sharom, 2008; Siarheyeva and Sharom, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that identified the exterior binding site.

claim: Introducing mutations to disrupt binding at the exterior site also abolishes lipid-induced stimulation of ATPase activity.
source: Similarly, introducing mutations to disrupt binding at the exterior site also abolishes lipid-induced stimulation of ATPase activity (Lyu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing effects of mutations at the exterior site.

claim: The mutant cycle method has proven to be highly effective in examining pairwise interactions, as demonstrated by its notable application in determining the spatial orientation of potassium channel residues in relation to high-affinity toxin binding.
source: The method has proven to be highly effective in examining pairwise interactions, as demonstrated by its notable application in determining the spatial orientation of potassium channel residues in relation to high-affinity toxin binding (Hidalgo and MacKinnon, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a classic study using mutant cycles.

claim: The ΔΔGint values for pairwise interactions in proteins has revealed the contributions of salt bridges (4–20 kJ/mol), aromatic-aromatic interactions (4 kJ/mol), and charge-aromatic interactions (4 kJ/mol) to protein stability.
source: The ΔΔGint values for pairwise interactions in proteins has revealed the contributions of salt bridges (4–20 kJ/mol), aromatic-aromatic interactions (4 kJ/mol), and charge-aromatic interactions (4 kJ/mol) to protein stability. (Horovitz, 1996; Luisi et al., 2003; Serrano et al., 1991)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that quantified different types of interactions using mutant cycles.

claim: Pairwise interactions between barnase and barstar residues that are less than seven angstrom in distance have been shown to be co-operative with coupling energies reaching as high as 7 kcal/mol.
source: For example, pairwise interactions between residues that are less than seven angstrom in distance (based on crystal structures) have been shown to be co-operative. These interactions were shown to be important for stability of the barnase-barstar complex with coupling energies reaching as high as 7 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is supported by the context discussing the barnase-barstar system as an example of mutant cycle analysis.

claim: One pair of residues (R24 from toxin and D431 from channel) in the scorpion toxin-Shaker potassium channel interaction displayed an extraordinary coupling energy of 17 kJ/mol.
source: Of the pairwise interactions that underwent mutant cycle analysis, one pair (R24 from toxin and D431 from channel) in particular displayed an extraordinary coupling energy of 17 kJ/mol.
evidence: This is supported by the context discussing the toxin-channel system as an example.

claim: Native mass spectrometry is capable of maintaining non-covalent interactions and native-like structure in the gas phase.
source: The technique is capable of maintaining non-covalent interactions and native-like structure in the gas phase (Ruotolo et al., 2005; Laganowsky et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating native MS capabilities.

claim: The molecular interaction between the signaling lipid 4,5-bisphosphate phosphatidylinositol and Kir3.2 is dominated by a large, favorable change in entropy.
source: For example, the molecular interaction between the signaling lipid 4,5-bisphosphate phosphatidylinositol and Kir3.2 is dominated by a large, favorable change in entropy (Qiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study that characterized Kir3.2-lipid interactions.

claim: The coupling energies determined by native MS and isothermal calorimetry are in agreement.
source: Notably, the coupling energies determined by native MS and isothermal calorimetry are in agreement (Sokolovski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study comparing native MS and ITC results.

claim: MsbA has two high-affinity binding sites for the LPS-precursor KDL.
source: It is established that MsbA has two high-affinity binding sites for the LPS-precursor KDL.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on prior structural and functional studies.

claim: R78 coordinates one of the characteristic phosphoglucosamine (P-GlcN) substituents of KDL whereas K299 interacts with a carboxylic acid group in the headgroup of KDL.
source: More specifically, R78 coordinates one of the characteristic phosphoglucosamine (P-GlcN) substituents of KDL whereas K299 interacts with a carboxylic acid group in the headgroup of KDL.
evidence: This is based on structural information about residue-lipid interactions.

claim: The two P-GlcN constituents of LOS are coordinated by R238 and R188 +K243, respectively.
source: The two P-GlcN constituents of LOS are coordinated by R238 and R188 +K243, respectively.
evidence: This is based on structural information about residue-lipid interactions.

claim: R188 forms an additional hydrogen bond with the headgroup of KDL.
source: R188 also forms an additional hydrogen bond with the headgroup of KDL.
evidence: This is based on structural information about residue-lipid interactions.

claim: Binding of KDL to MsbA was enhanced at higher temperatures.
source: For example, binding of KDL to MsbA was enhanced at higher temperatures (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3), indicating a favorable entropy for the interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures from temperature-dependent binding studies.

claim: van' t Hoff analysis showed a non-linear trend for three KDL binding reactions, indicating that over the selected temperature range, heat capacity is not constant.
source: Interestingly, van' t Hoff analysis showed a non-linear trend for three KDL binding reactions (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3), indicating that over the selected temperature range, heat capacity is not constant (Prabhu and Sharp, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in van't Hoff plots and cited literature on heat capacity.

claim: ΔG values for binding KDL1-2 range from –32.0±0.1 to -35.2±0.1 kJ/mol.
source: ΔG values for binding KDL1-2 range from –32.0±0.1 to -35.2±0.1 kJ/mol.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data.

claim: At the lowest temperature, KDL binding is driven by favorable enthalpy (–36±12 to -43±7 kJ/mol) with a small entropically penalty (-TΔS, 2±11–12±7 kJ/mol at 288 K).
source: At the lowest temperature, KDL binding is driven by favorable enthalpy (–36±12 to -43±7 kJ/mol) with a small entropically penalty (-TΔS, 2±11–12±7 kJ/mol at 288 K).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements.

claim: KDL binding at higher temperatures displays a large, favorable entropy (-TΔS, –123±12 to -146±7 kJ/mol at 303 K) that compensates a large enthalpic barrier (86±12–112±7 kJ/mol).
source: In contrast, KDL binding at higher temperatures displays a large, favorable entropy (-TΔS, –123±12 to -146±7 kJ/mol at 303 K) that compensates a large enthalpic barrier (86±12–112±7 kJ/mol).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements.

claim: MsbAR78A showed a reduction in binding KDL1-2 with ΔG ranging from –30.2±0.2 to -32.5±0.2 kJ/mol.
source: MsbAR78A showed a reduction in binding KDL1-2 with ΔG ranging from –30.2±0.2 to -32.5±0.2 kJ/mol.
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on the mutant protein.

claim: At 298 K, KDL binding to MsbAR78A is enthalpically and entropically favorable whereas binding of the second KDL is similar to the wild-type protein.
source: At 298 K, KDL binding is enthalpically and entropically favorable whereas binding of the second KDL is similar to the wild-type protein (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements shown in figures.

claim: The binding thermodynamics for MsbAK299A is reminiscent of the wild-type protein with a large, favorable change in entropy (-TΔS, –75±2 to -86±1 kJ/mol at 298 K) and unfavorable enthalpy (43±2–53±1 kJ/mol).
source: The binding thermodynamics for MsbAK299A is reminiscent of the wild-type protein with a large, favorable change in entropy (-TΔS, –75±2 to -86±1 kJ/mol at 298 K) and unfavorable enthalpy (43±2–53±1 kJ/mol) (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements shown in figures.

claim: The double mutant MsbAR78A,K299A protein shows a reduction in opposing entropic and enthalpic terms leading to an increase in ΔG by ~4 kJ/mol relative to wild-type MsbA.
source: The double mutant MsbAR78A,K299A protein shows a reduction in opposing entropic and enthalpic terms leading to an increase in ΔG by ~4 kJ/mol relative to wild-type MsbA (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on the double mutant protein.

claim: Mutant cycle analysis indicates a coupling energy (ΔΔGint) of 1.7±0.4 kJ/mol that contributes to the stability of KDL-MsbA complex for R78 and K299.
source: Mutant cycle analysis indicates a coupling energy (ΔΔGint) of 1.7±0.4 kJ/mol that contributes to the stability of KDL-MsbA complex (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3 and Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: The coupling enthalpy (ΔΔHint of –26±15 kJ/mol) and coupling entropy (Δ(-TΔS)int of 28±15 kJ/mol at 298 K) for R78 and K299 indicate that these residues contribute to KDL binding through an entropy driven process that overcomes an enthalpic barrier.
source: Interestingly, the coupling enthalpy (ΔΔHint of –26±15 kJ/mol) and coupling entropy (Δ(-TΔS)int of 28±15 kJ/mol at 298 K) indicating that these residues contribute to KDL binding through an entropy driven process that overcomes an enthalpic barrier (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3 and Table 3).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental thermodynamic data.

claim: Both MsbAR188A and MsbAK243A single mutants marginally weakened the interaction by about 2 kJ/mol.
source: Both MsbAR188A and MsbAK243A single mutants marginally weakened the interaction by about 2 kJ/mol (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on mutant proteins.

claim: The R238A mutation significantly weakened the interaction with KDL, increasing ΔG by nearly 5 kJ/mol compared to the wild-type transporter.
source: However, the R238A mutation significantly weakened the interaction with KDL, increasing ΔG by nearly 5 kJ/mol compared to the wild-type transporter (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 3)
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on the mutant protein.

claim: R238A mutation resulted in a distinct thermodynamic pattern with negative enthalpy changes for both the first and second KDL binding events.
source: However, the R238A mutation significantly weakened the interaction with KDL, increasing ΔG by nearly 5 kJ/mol compared to the wild-type transporter (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 3) and resulted in an distinct thermodynamic pattern with negative enthalpy changes for both the first and second KDL binding events (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements on the mutant protein.

claim: ΔG for MsbAR188A,K243A was comparable to the K243A single mutant form of the protein.
source: ΔG for MsbAR188A,K243A was comparable to the K243A single mutant form of the protein (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements comparing mutant proteins.

claim: The positive coupling energy for R188A and K243A is 3.2±0.4 kJ/mol with contributions from a coupling enthalpy of 19±11 kJ/mol and a coupling entropy of –16±12 kJ/mol at 298 K.
source: The positive coupling energy of 3.2±0.4 kJ/mol with contributions from a coupling enthalpy of 19±11 kJ/mol and a coupling entropy of –16±12 kJ/mol at 298 K (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 3).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: Combining mutation R238A with R188A, MsbAR188A,R238A decreased ΔH by 57 kJ/mol at the cost of increasing -TΔS by 64 kJ/mol at 298 K.
source: Combining mutation R238A with R188A, MsbAR188A,R238A decreased ΔH by 57 kJ/mol at the cost of increasing -TΔS by 64 kJ/mol at 298 K (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 3).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements on the double mutant protein.

claim: The coupling energy for R188A and R238A is approximately zero as a result of equal coupling enthalpy and entropy of different signs.
source: The coupling energy for R188A and R238A is approximately zero as a result of equal coupling enthalpy and entropy of different signs.
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: MsbAR238A,K243A results in an inversion of the thermodynamic signature with binding now being driven by enthalpy, accompanied by ΔΔH and Δ(-TΔS) of –93±7 kJ/mol and 99±7 kJ/mol at 298 K.
source: Compared to the wild-type protein, MsbAR238A,K243A results in an inversion of the thermodynamic signature with binding now being driven by enthalpy. More specifically, this inversion is accompanied by ΔΔH and Δ(-TΔS) of –93±7 kJ/mol and 99±7 kJ/mol at 298 K (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 3).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements on the double mutant protein.

claim: The coupling enthalpy and entropy for R238A and R243A are of equal magnitude but opposite signs, giving rise to a coupling energy of zero.
source: Again, the coupling enthalpy and entropy (at 298 K) of equal magnitude but opposite signs give rise to a coupling energy of zero for R238A and R243A (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 3).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: Introduction of the R188A mutation into MsbAR238A,K243A results in reversal of the thermodynamic signature to mirror that of MsbAR188A,K243A.
source: Introduction of the R188A mutation into MsbAR238A,K243A, results in reversal of the thermodynamic signature to mirror that of MsbAR188A,K243A (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements on the triple mutant protein.

claim: The coupling energy, coupling enthalpy, and coupling entropy for R188A, R238A, and R243A are 3.4±0.5 kJ/mol, 100±16 kJ/mol, and –97±16 kJ/mol at 298 K, respectively.
source: The coupling energy, coupling enthalpy, and coupling entropy for R188A, R238A, and R243A are 3.4±0.5 kJ/mol, 100±16 kJ/mol, and –97±16 kJ/mol at 298 K (Table 4), respectively.
evidence: This is derived from triple mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: MsbA containing single mutations (MsbAR188A,K299A) at both LOS binding sites resulted in the greatest change in ΔG.
source: Of the mutant proteins, MsbA containing single mutations (MsbAR188A,K299A) at both LOS binding sites resulted in the greatest change in ΔG.
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements comparing different mutant proteins.

claim: Mutations at either the interior or exterior sites have a direct impact of KDL binding to MsbA.
source: Here, we find mutations at either the interior or exterior sites have a direct impact of KDL binding to MsbA, which under these conditions is presumably adopting an open, IF conformation.
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on various mutant proteins.

claim: The interior and exterior LOS binding sites are allosterically coupled.
source: This result implies that these sites are allosterically coupled and further investigation is warranted to better understand how the exterior LOS binding sites influence MsbA dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations at one site affect binding at the other site.

claim: Thermodynamics of MsbA(KDL)1-2 binding in the vanadate-trapped state is like the non-trapped transporter, wherein entropy (-TΔS ranging from –58±1 to -69±1 kJ/mol at 298 K) is more favorable than a positive enthalpic term (ΔH ranging from 22±1–35±1 kJ/mol).
source: Thermodynamics of MsbA(KDL)1-2 binding is like the non-trapped transporter, wherein entropy (-TΔS ranging from –58±1 to -69±1 kJ/mol at 298 K) is more favorable than a positive enthalpic term (ΔH ranging from 22±1–35±1 kJ/mol) (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements on vanadate-trapped MsbA.

claim: The single mutant proteins (MsbAR188A, MsbAR238A, and MsbAK243A) in the vanadate-trapped state showed a slight increase in ΔG (at most 5 kJ/mol).
source: The single mutant proteins (MsbAR188A, MsbAR238A, and MsbAK243A) showed a slight increase in ΔG (at most 5 kJ/mol) (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on vanadate-trapped mutant proteins.

claim: MsbAR238A and MsbAK243A in the vanadate-trapped state had about a four-fold increase in ΔH and favorable entropy was about two-fold higher.
source: Notably, we found MsbAR238A and MsbAK243A had about a four-fold increase in ΔH and favorable entropy was about two-fold higher (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements on vanadate-trapped mutant proteins.

claim: Double mutant cycle analysis of the pairwise mutants in the vanadate-trapped state revealed a positive coupling energy of ~2 kJ/mol for MsbA binding one and two KDLs.
source: Double mutant cycle analysis of the pairwise mutants revealed a positive coupling energy of ~2 kJ/mol for MsbA binding one and two KDLs (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6 and Table 7).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data on vanadate-trapped MsbA.

claim: For the first KDL binding event in vanadate-trapped MsbA, the coupling enthalpy and coupling entropy at 298 K for R188 and K238 was 89±7 kJ/mol and –87±7 kJ/mol, respectively.
source: Focusing on the first KDL binding event, the coupling enthalpy and coupling entropy at 298 K for R188 and K238 was 89±7 kJ/mol and –87±7 kJ/mol, respectively (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6 and Tables 7 and 8).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data on vanadate-trapped MsbA.

claim: R238 and K243 in vanadate-trapped MsbA showed 129±11 kJ/mol of coupling enthalpy and –127±11 kJ/mol of coupling entropy at 298 K.
source: Likewise, R238 and K243 showed 129±11 kJ/mol of coupling enthalpy and –127±11 kJ/mol of coupling entropy at 298 K (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6 and Tables 7 and 8).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data on vanadate-trapped MsbA.

claim: The R188 and K243 pair in vanadate-trapped MsbA revealed a relatively low coupling enthalpy and coupling entropy at 298 K of 3.5±7 kJ/mol and 2±7 kJ/mol, respectively.
source: However, the R188 and K243 pair revealed a relatively low coupling enthalpy and coupling entropy at 298 K of 3.5±7 kJ/mol and 2±7 kJ/mol, respectively (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–6 and Tables 7 and 8).
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data on vanadate-trapped MsbA.

claim: A recurring thermodynamic strategy for specific KDL-MsbA interactions is a large, favorable entropic term that opposes a positive enthalpic value.
source: A recurring thermodynamic strategy for specific KDL-MsbA interactions is a large, favorable entropic term that opposes a positive enthalpic value.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the thermodynamic data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The human G-protein-gated inward rectifier potassium channel (Kir3.2) used a similar thermodynamic strategy to engage phosphoinositides (PIPs).
source: The human G-protein-gated inward rectifier potassium channel (Kir3.2) also used a similar thermodynamic strategy to engage phosphoinositides (PIPs) (Qiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Kir3.2-PIP interactions.

claim: The large, positive entropy could stem from solvent reorganization of the lipid with a carbohydrate containing headgroup, and desolvation of hydrated binding pockets on the membrane protein.
source: The large, positive entropy could stem from solvent reorganization of the lipid with a carbohydrate containing headgroup, and desolvation of hydrated binding pockets on the membrane protein.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the thermodynamic data.

claim: The release of ordered solvent to the bulk solvent would contribute favorably to entropy.
source: The release of ordered solvent to the bulk solvent would contribute favorably to entropy.
evidence: This is based on established thermodynamic principles applied to the observed data.

claim: Soluble protein-ligand interactions can be driven by a large, positive entropy term that outweighs a large, positive enthalpic penalty, mainly driven by conformational entropy originating in enhanced protein motions.
source: Previous work has shown soluble protein-ligand interactions can be driven by a large, positive entropy term that outweighs a large, positive enthalpic penalty (Frederick et al., 2007; Tzeng and Kalodimos, 2009; Tzeng and Kalodimos, 2012; Caro et al., 2017). In these cases, the reaction is mainly driven by conformational entropy originating in enhanced protein motions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on soluble protein-ligand interactions.

claim: It is unclear if the conformational dynamics of MsbA are enhanced when bound to KDL.
source: However, it is unclear if the conformational dynamics of MsbA are enhanced when bound to KDL.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the data.

claim: In nearly all cases, a positive ΔCp was observed that ranged in value from 4 to 12 kJ/mol·K.
source: In nearly all cases, a positive ΔCp was observed that ranged in value from 4 to 12 kJ/mol·K (Tables 2 and 6).
evidence: This is derived from experimental thermodynamic measurements.

claim: Solvation of polar groups in aqueous solvent has been ascribed to positive heat capacities whereas the collapse of apolar residues from their solvated state is accompanied by a negative change in heat capacity.
source: Solvation of polar groups in aqueous solvent has been ascribed to positive heat capacities whereas the collapse of apolar residues from their solvated state is accompanied by a negative change in heat capacity (Prabhu and Sharp, 2005; Makhatadze and Privalov, 1995).
evidence: This is established thermodynamic knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Reorganization of the hydrated, polar headgroups of KD is consistent with the positive heat capacity observed.
source: Reorganization of the hydrated, polar headgroups of KD is consistent with the positive heat capacity observed here.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data based on established thermodynamic principles.

claim: Change in heat capacity could also be ascribed to temperature-dependent conformational changes in MsbA and/or KDL.
source: However, change in heat capacity could also be ascribed to temperature-dependent conformational changes in MsbA and/or KDL.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: Vanadate-trapped MsbA locked in an open, OF conformation should be less conformationally dynamic than the apo protein.
source: Notably, vanadate-trapped MsbA locked in an open, OF conformation should be less conformationally dynamic than the apo protein, which is known to adopt a number of open, IF conformations where the NBDs are separated by different distances.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of MsbA conformational states.

claim: Similar positive heat capacities were observed for the different conformations, suggesting the dynamics of MsbA marginally contribute to the observed non-linear trends.
source: Similar positive heat capacities were observed for the different conformations, suggesting the dynamics of MsbA marginally contribute to the observed non-linear trends.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing experimental data from different MsbA conformational states.

claim: The headgroup of KDL is nestled in a hydrophilic, basic patch of MsbA in the open, OF conformation.
source: Notably, the headgroup of KDL is nestled in a hydrophilic, basic patch of MsbA in the open, OF conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural information.

claim: The headgroup of PIP binds a hydrophilic, basic pocket in Kir3.2.
source: Similarly, the headgroup of PIP binds a hydrophilic, basic pocket in Kir3.2.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from cited literature.

claim: These hydrophilic patches will be highly solvated, which will be desolvated upon binding lipids contributing favorably to entropy.
source: These hydrophilic patches will be highly solvated, which will be desolvated upon binding lipids contributing favorably to entropy.
evidence: This is an inference based on thermodynamic principles and structural information.

claim: Phospholipid binding to the bacterial ammonia channel (AmtB) were largely driven by enthalpy and, in most cases, entropy was unfavorable.
source: Phospholipid binding to the bacterial ammonia channel (AmtB) were largely driven by enthalpy and, in most cases, entropy was unfavorable (Cong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on AmtB-lipid interactions.

claim: Significant enthalpy-entropy compensation was observed for each sequential lipid binding event to AmtB.
source: Another interesting observation for AmtB-lipid interactions was significant enthalpy-entropy compensation for each sequential lipid binding event.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on AmtB-lipid interactions.

claim: Enthalpy-entropy compensation is not as pronounced in MsbA-KDL interactions.
source: Here, enthalpy-entropy compensation is not as pronounced.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the current data to AmtB data.

claim: The difference in enthalpy-entropy compensation may reflect the much higher affinity and specific MsbA-KDL interactions compared to the weaker AmtB-lipid interactions.
source: This result may reflect the much higher affinity and specific MsbA-KDL interactions compared to the weaker AmtB-lipid interactions, sometimes referred to as non-annular lipids (Bolla et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation comparing different protein-lipid systems.

claim: It is presently thought that flipping of LOS occurs at interior MsbA site, and the exterior LOS binding site enables feedforward activation, wherein binding of LOS and precursors thereof stimulates ATPase activity.
source: It is presently thought that flipping of LOS occurs at interior MsbA site, and the exterior LOS binding site enables feedforward activation, wherein binding of LOS and precursors thereof stimulates ATPase activity (Mi et al., 2017; Ho et al., 2018; Lyu et al., 2022; Gorzelak et al., 2021; Ward et al., 2007; Zou and McHaourab, 2009; Dong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on current understanding from cited literature.

claim: Binding of LOS and ATP promotes dimerization of the NBDs.
source: It is also thought that binding of LOS and ATP promotes dimerization of the NBDs.
evidence: This is based on current understanding from literature.

claim: Mutations at either the interior or exterior sites have a direct impact of KDL binding to MsbA, which under these conditions is presumably adopting an open, IF conformation.
source: Here, we find mutations at either the interior or exterior sites have a direct impact of KDL binding to MsbA, which under these conditions is presumably adopting an open, IF conformation.
evidence: This is derived from experimental measurements on mutant proteins.

claim: Double mutants targeting the interior site reveal a positive coupling energy of nearly 2 kJ/mol for R78 and K299.
source: Double mutants targeting the interior site reveal a positive coupling energy of nearly 2 kJ/mol for R78 and K299.
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: R78 and K299 stabilize the MsbA-KDL complex largely through nearly 17 kJ/mol of favorable coupling entropy, which outweighs a negative coupling enthalpy.
source: These stabilize the MsbA-KDL complex largely through nearly 17 kJ/mol of favorable coupling entropy, which outweighs a negative coupling enthalpy.
evidence: This is derived from mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: The largest coupling energy is observed from the triple mutant cycle of R188A, R238A, and R243A, with stabilization of the complex achieved via favorable coupling entropy.
source: The largest coupling energy is observed from the triple mutant cycle of R188A, R238A, and R243A, which again stabilization of the complex was achieved via favorable coupling entropy.
evidence: This is derived from triple mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: The coupling energetics among R188, R238, and R243 show 3.4±0.5 kJ/mol at 298 K.
source: While we focused on results at 298 K, the coupling energetics among these three residues show 3.4±0.5 kJ/mol.
evidence: This is derived from triple mutant cycle analysis of experimental data.

claim: Mutant cycle analysis reveals that entropy drives high-affinity KDL binding to MsbA and solvent reorganization contributes to KDL binding.
source: Taken together, mutant cycle analysis reveals that entropy drives high-affinity KDL binding to MsbA and solvent reorganization contributes to KDL binding (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the mutant cycle analysis data.

claim: There are many factors that contribute to the change in entropy of the system, beyond solvation entropy.
source: There are many factors that contribute to the change in entropy of the system, beyond solvation entropy, and deciphering the entropic contributions of the various components warrants additional studies.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in interpreting the entropic contributions.

claim: Native MS coupled with a variable-temperature nanoelectrospray ionization (nESI) apparatus has been used to ascertain equilibrium binding constants and thermodynamic properties of protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions.
source: Native MS coupled with a variable-temperature nanoelectrospray ionization (nESI) apparatus (McCabe et al., 2021; Cong et al., 2016) has been used to ascertain equilibrium binding constants and thermodynamic properties of protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using this technique.

claim: The results obtained by native MS align closely with those obtained through other biophysical techniques, such as isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR).
source: The results obtained align closely with those obtained through other biophysical techniques, such as isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) (Cong et al., 2017; Daneshfar et al., 2004; Daneshfar et al., 2004; Cong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to validation studies.

claim: Native MS has uncovered that specific protein-lipid interactions can allosterically modulate other interactions with protein, lipid, and drug molecules.
source: The approach has also uncovered that specific protein-lipid interactions can allosterically modulate other interactions with protein, lipid, and drug molecules (Marcoux et al., 2013; Yen et al., 2018; Cong et al., 2017; Patrick et al., 2018; Bolla et al., 2018; Gault et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing allosteric effects.

claim: Native MS has proved useful in dissecting the thermodynamics of individual nucleotide binding events to GroEL, a 801 kDa tetradecameric chaperonin.
source: More recently, native MS has proved useful in dissecting the thermodynamics of individual nucleotide binding events to GroEL, a 801 kDa tetradecameric chaperonin (Walker et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on GroEL.

claim: Unlike traditional approaches, native MS can resolve and dissect individual binding events enabling the measurement of binding thermodynamics.
source: In contrast to traditional approaches, such as ITC and SPR, native MS can resolve and dissect individual binding events enabling the measurement of binding thermodynamics, which is of paramount importance to understanding the molecular driving forces of non-covalent interactions.
evidence: This is based on the capabilities of native MS demonstrated in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: A similar thermodynamic strategy was also observed for Kir3.2-PIP interactions, where entropy plays a central role in the wild-type channel recognizing PIP.
source: A similar thermodynamic strategy was also observed for Kir3.2-PIP interactions, where entropy plays a central role in the wild-type channel recognizing PIP (Qiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Kir3.2-PIP interactions.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that favorable entropy is a common theme enabling membrane proteins to specifically engage carbohydrate-containing lipids.
source: It is tempting to speculate that favorable entropy is a common theme enabling membrane proteins to specifically engage carbohydrate-containing lipids.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the current data and comparison to Kir3.2.

claim: Thermodynamics and mutant cycles will be invaluable in not only better understanding high-affinity lipid binding sites but also in the development of inhibitors, such as those that may target specific protein-lipid binding site(s).
source: We envision thermodynamics and mutant cycles will be invaluable in not only better understanding high-affinity lipid binding sites but also in the development of inhibitors, such as those that may target specific protein-lipid binding site(s).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential applications.

claim: These studies provide deeper insight into the thermodynamic strategies membrane proteins exploit to achieve high-affinity lipid binding site(s).
source: In closing, these studies provide deeper insight into the thermodynamic strategies membrane proteins exploit to achieve high-affinity lipid binding site(s).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.

claim: Native mass spectrometry can resolve different ligand bound states, including the free concentration of protein and free concentration of ligand(s), in a single mass spectrum.
source: It is important to note that, unlike traditional approaches that struggle to distinguish between free protein from that bound to ligand, (Jarmoskaite et al., 2020) native MS can resolve different ligand bound states, including the free concentration of protein and free concentration of ligand(s), in a single mass spectrum (Daneshfar et al., 2004; Cong et al., 2016; Cong et al., 2017; Patrick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this capability of native MS.

claim: The native MS approach has been cross validated using isothermal calorimetry and surface plasmon resonance.
source: Notably, the native MS approach has been cross validated using isothermal calorimetry and surface plasmon resonance (Daneshfar et al., 2004; Cong et al., 2016; Cong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to validation studies.

claim: The transporter was stable at the selected temperatures for the thermodynamic measurements.
source: The transporter was stable at the selected temperatures.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions and protein stability.

claim: MsbA samples used for native MS studies do not contain any co-purified LPS.
source: These studies used optimized samples of MsbA that do not contain any co-purified LPS (for details see Lyu et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the sample preparation and is supported by citation to methods.
